readings.title: The Children of the Night
readings.challenge: Follow an argument in verse: find its “if” and its “but,” and where it finally lands.
readings.focus: Robinson asks what hope there is for people who live in darkness, and answers with a call to courage.
readings.context: Edwin Arlington Robinson (1869–1935) was in his twenties, poor and grieving for his parents, when he published this book in 1897; it takes its name from this poem, which argues about faith and suffering. Winnowing is tossing grain in the wind to separate it from chaff; circumstance means chance and situation; creeds are statements of religious belief; a fiend is a devil; sublime means awe-inspiringly grand; to revere is to honour deeply. “Honest doubt” echoes Tennyson’s famous line that there is more faith in honest doubt than in half the creeds.
readings.contentNote: The poem considers the idea that, without hope, it would be better to drown at the start of life than to live in darkness, and then argues against that despair.

excerpt.locator: “The Children of the Night,” complete poem; opens “For those that never know the light, The darkness is a sullen thing; And they, the…”; closes “…that hides the scar! Let us be Children of the Light, And tell the ages what we are!”.

questions.prompt: Who are “the Children of the Night” in the first two stanzas, and what has shut them out?
facilitatorNotes: People who “never know the light,” for whom life is dark: the weak, the unlucky, the homeless, sorted by chance as grain is sorted by the wind. Countless hearts seek a refuge that never comes.
evidence: For those that never know the light, The darkness is a sullen thing;
Are shut from countless hearts that seek World-refuge that will never come.

questions.prompt: Stanzas three to five depend on “if.” What would be true, the speaker says, if this life were the only chance?
facilitatorNotes: If there were no other life and only chance decided our sorrows, it would be better to drown at the start of the voyage than to sail forever in the dark. The “if” marks this as a possibility he is testing, not his conclusion; the poem goes on to answer it.
evidence: And if there be no other life,
In life's imbittered sea to drown, Than sail forever in the dark.

questions.prompt: What kind of belief does the speaker reject in the middle of the poem, and what “creed” does he put in its place?
facilitatorNotes: He rejects creeds that “make a fiend” of God, beliefs that picture God as cruel; if God is God, He is just and He is Love. In their place he offers “the common creed of common sense.” Some readers find that too vague to comfort anyone; others find it honest.
evidence: With creeds that make a fiend of Him.
The common creed of common sense.

questions.prompt: Explain “the crimson, not the gray” and “the faith within the fear.” Why does the poem end by calling us “Children of the Light”?
facilitatorNotes: Crimson is dawn’s colour: hope, not dull gray, is what makes twilight beautiful, and the promise of day makes the night sky grand. Even inside fear there is faith that keeps people living. So the speaker urges sufferers to stop hiding their scars and to face the world openly, as children of light.
evidence: It is the faith within the fear That holds us to the life we curse;
Put off the cloak that hides the scar!

readings.title: The World
readings.challenge: Sort the poem’s pairs of opposites, then test its final claim.
readings.focus: The world looks different depending on who is looking.
readings.context: Edwin Arlington Robinson sets different kinds of people side by side in three short stanzas. Estate here means a person’s condition in life; enmity is hostility; unguarded means unprotected; an under-song is a low sound beneath a melody; the Scheme is the plan of the universe; luminous means shining; chaos is total disorder.

excerpt.locator: “The World,” complete poem; opens “Some are the brothers of all humankind, And own them, whatsoever their estate; And some,…”; closes “…And so 't is what we are that makes for us The measure and the meaning of the world.”.

questions.prompt: The first stanza describes two kinds of people. What are they, and what makes the second kind “blind”?
facilitatorNotes: Some treat all humankind as brothers, whatever their condition. Others, blinded by sorrow and self-scorn, feel hostility towards everyone. Unhappiness with oneself turns into hatred of others.
evidence: Some are the brothers of all humankind,
And some, for sorrow and self-scorn, are blind

questions.prompt: What do the flutes and the “under-song” in the second stanza stand for?
facilitatorNotes: For some, life sounds like flutes in Paradise because they are glad; for others it is the “eternal under-song” of curses and madness. An under-song runs beneath the melody, so it may be there for everyone, though only some hear it.
evidence: Like flutes in Paradise, they are so glad;
And there is hell's eternal under-song

questions.prompt: Each stanza is built on “some … and some.” Why might Robinson hold back his own view until the last two lines?
facilitatorNotes: He sets the opposites out fairly first, so the conclusion seems earned: the differences lie in the people, not the world. Even the universe divides people, some seeing it “luminous” with love and some wishing it back in chaos.
evidence: Some say the Scheme with love stands luminous,

questions.prompt: Put the last two lines in your own words. Do you agree?
facilitatorNotes: What we are decides what the world means to us. Agreeing: attitude shapes experience. Disagreeing: some suffering is real whatever your outlook, such as poverty or illness, and the claim could seem to blame sufferers. Good answers use the poem’s own examples.
evidence: And so 't is what we are that makes for us The measure and the meaning of the world.

readings.title: An Old Story
readings.challenge: Work out exactly why the speaker hated his friend, and why he understands only now.
readings.focus: A confession of envy that came too late to put right.
readings.context: Edwin Arlington Robinson wrote many short poems about friendship and regret. Envy is resentment of someone else’s success or good qualities.

excerpt.locator: “An Old Story,” complete poem; opens “Strange that I did not know him then, That friend of mine! I did not even show him then…”; closes “…the earth of him Once, in my pride! . . . I never knew the worth of him Until he died.”.

questions.prompt: What did the friend do that made the speaker curse him? Read the second stanza slowly.
facilitatorNotes: The friend praised the speaker, and people praised the friend for being so generous. That praise made the speaker envious, and showed him his own envy. He hated the friend for making him see something ugly in himself.
evidence: But cursed him for the ways he had To make me see
My envy of the praise he had For praising me.

questions.prompt: Why does the speaker call it “Strange” that he did not know his friend then?
facilitatorNotes: The man was his friend all along, yet he never showed him one friendly sign. Only looking back does he see who the man was; “know” here means understand and value.
evidence: Strange that I did not know him then, That friend of mine!

questions.prompt: Look at the rhymes: “know him then” and “show him then,” “rid the earth of him” and “the worth of him.” What does rhyming on nearly the same words do?
facilitatorNotes: The lines echo each other, like someone going over the same memory again and again. The last pair sets opposites side by side: once he wanted the man gone from the earth, now he knows the man’s worth.
evidence: I would have rid the earth of him
I never knew the worth of him

questions.prompt: Why might the poem be called “An Old Story”?
facilitatorNotes: It happened long ago and the friend is dead; and it is an old, common story, since people often value someone only after losing them, and envy of a friend is as old as friendship. Readers may also hear the speaker’s weariness with his own regret.
evidence: Until he died.

readings.title: Luke Havergal
readings.challenge: Work out who is speaking and what the voice urges, while keeping open what the poem never states.
readings.focus: A voice from the grave offers a grieving man a way forward that sounds both comforting and dangerous.
readings.context: Edwin Arlington Robinson (1869–1935) grew up in Gardiner, Maine, and many poems in this early book portray people of a small New England town. An unnamed voice speaks to Luke Havergal, who has lost the woman he loves. Rift means split open; quench means put out; riddle here means puzzle out.
readings.contentNote: A voice speaks from the grave to a grieving man. Many readers hear in its “one way to where she is” a hint of death, even suicide; the poem never says so, and adults may want to be ready to talk about it.

excerpt.locator: “Luke Havergal,” complete poem; opens “Go to the western gate, Luke Havergal, -- There where the vines cling crimson on the…”; closes “…you trust her she will call. There is the western gate, Luke Havergal -- Luke Havergal.”.

questions.prompt: Where is Luke told to go, and which details of that place return at the end?
facilitatorNotes: The western gate, where crimson vines cling to the wall and leaves fall at twilight. The last stanza repeats the gate, the leaves and the promise almost word for word, so the instruction sounds like a summons or a spell.
evidence: Go to the western gate, Luke Havergal,
There where the vines cling crimson on the wall,

questions.prompt: Who speaks in the third stanza, and how does that change the advice you heard in the first?
facilitatorNotes: The voice comes “Out of a grave”: it may be the dead woman or another spirit. Advice from the dead about reaching the dead is less reassuring than it first sounded; some readers find it loving, others sinister.
evidence: Out of a grave I come to tell you this,

questions.prompt: Why does the voice deny Luke a dawn in the east and point him west?
facilitatorNotes: East is sunrise and a new day; west is sunset and ending. The voice refuses him a fresh start and says only darkness can end his darkness. Readers may hear patience, faith or despair in that line.
evidence: No, there is not a dawn in eastern skies
The dark will end the dark, if anything:

questions.prompt: What is the “one way to where she is”? Separate what the poem states from what readers guess.
facilitatorNotes: Stated: the way is bitter and needs faith. Guessed: it could mean waiting faithfully until his own death, keeping faith with her memory, or something more dangerous. The poem refuses to choose, and a careful answer says so.
evidence: Yes, there is yet one way to where she is
Bitter, but one that faith can never miss.

readings.title: The House on the Hill
readings.challenge: Track two repeating lines and decide what changes each time they return.
readings.focus: Repetition turns a short statement of loss into the speakers’ inability to stop circling it.
readings.context: Edwin Arlington Robinson wrote this as a villanelle, an old French form of nineteen lines in which two lines come back again and again. A sill is the ledge at the foot of a door or window; fancy-play means imagining.

excerpt.locator: “The House on the Hill,” complete poem; opens “They are all gone away, The House is shut and still, There is nothing more to say.”; closes “…and decay In the House on the Hill: They are all gone away, There is nothing more to say.”.

questions.prompt: Follow the two refrains. Where do they finally stand together, and what does that do to the ending?
facilitatorNotes: “They are all gone away” and “There is nothing more to say” take turns, then stand side by side in the last stanza. Joined, they close the poem as if no more words could follow.
evidence: They are all gone away, There is nothing more to say.

questions.prompt: If there is “nothing more to say,” why do the speakers keep returning to the house?
facilitatorNotes: They admit it is empty, yet they still “stray” around it and imagine its people. The refrain claims silence while the form keeps repeating it, which shows memory or grief that will not settle. Some readers find the visitors foolish, others loyal.
evidence: Why is it then we stray
Around that sunken sill?

questions.prompt: Who are “they,” and who is “we”? What does the poem gain by never telling us?
facilitatorNotes: No names and no story of why the people left or died. Leaving them unnamed lets the house stand for any lost home or past, and the speakers themselves call their imagining “wasted skill.”
evidence: And our poor fancy-play
For them is wasted skill:

readings.title: Richard Cory
readings.challenge: Notice who is telling the story and what they could not see.
readings.focus: A whole town’s admiration rests on surfaces, and the last line shows how little it knew.
readings.context: Edwin Arlington Robinson’s portraits of a small New England town often look at a neighbour from outside. Here “we” are the town’s working people. Clean favored means good-looking; arrayed means dressed; in fine means in short.
readings.contentNote: The last line tells, without detail, that a man shot himself. Adults may want to be ready to talk about suicide.

excerpt.locator: “Richard Cory,” complete poem; opens “Whenever Richard Cory went down town, We people on the pavement looked at him: He was a…”; closes “…And Richard Cory, one calm summer night, Went home and put a bullet through his head.”.

questions.prompt: List what the townspeople admire about Richard Cory. Which of these could they actually see or hear?
facilitatorNotes: His looks, clothes, manners, greeting, wealth and schooling: all public surfaces. They watch him from the pavement, and nothing they report comes from inside his life.
evidence: We people on the pavement looked at him:
and he glittered when he walked.

questions.prompt: Which words make him sound royal, and why might the speakers reach for them?
facilitatorNotes: “from sole to crown,” “imperially slim,” “richer than a king.” Royal words show how far above themselves the townspeople place him; they may also hint at the distance between him and everyone else.
evidence: He was a gentleman from sole to crown,
richer than a king

questions.prompt: What does the third stanza tell us about the speakers’ own lives, and why does it come just before the end?
facilitatorNotes: They work, wait “for the light,” go without meat and curse the bread. The contrast suggests they assume money and grace would end their troubles; the last line contradicts that assumption at once.
evidence: So on we worked, and waited for the light,
And went without the meat, and cursed the bread;

questions.prompt: The poem gives no reason for its ending. Is that a weakness or the point?
facilitatorNotes: A strong answer: the silence is the point, because the town never knew him and neither do we. Others may want a cause; that wish is worth discussing, as long as the discussion stays with what watching from outside cannot show.
evidence: one calm summer night,
To make us wish that we were in his place.

readings.title: Amaryllis
readings.challenge: Read a sonnet twice: once as a story about an old man, once as a poem about poetry.
readings.focus: In a modern age, even the shepherdess of the old poems has grown old.
readings.context: Amaryllis is a name from pastoral poetry, old verse about shepherds and shepherdesses in an imagined countryside of love and song; the Roman poet Virgil and the English poet Milton both used it for a beautiful young woman. Edwin Arlington Robinson wrote in the 1890s, a loud age of factories, railways and trade. A complaint here is a sad song; a quaver is a trembling voice; commerce is buying and selling.
readings.contentNote: An old man shows the speaker the body of an old woman he has buried.

excerpt.locator: “Amaryllis,” complete poem; opens “Once, when I wandered in the woods alone, An old man tottered up to me and said, "Come,…”; closes “…were glad, It made me lonely and it made me sad To think that Amaryllis had grown old.”.

questions.prompt: What happens in the first eight lines? What does the speaker find at the grave?
facilitatorNotes: An old man totters up and asks him to see the grave he has made for Amaryllis; moved by pity, the speaker goes, and sees an ancient woman, “shrunk to skin and bone.” The name promises youth and beauty; the body is old and withered.
evidence: Come, friend, and see the grave that I have made For Amaryllis.
An ancient woman, shrunk to skin and bone.

questions.prompt: What sounds come from beyond the forest, and how do they differ from the old man’s voice?
facilitatorNotes: Loud progress, the “bold / Incessant scream of commerce,” the glad trumpets of the world: confident, noisy, never stopping. Against them the old man’s quavering lament is small and private.
evidence: The calling of loud progress, and the bold Incessant scream of commerce ringing clear;

questions.prompt: Why does the thought that “Amaryllis had grown old” make the speaker lonely and sad while the world is glad?
facilitatorNotes: Amaryllis never ages in poems; if she has grown old, the old dream of beauty and simple song has died, and the busy modern world does not notice or care. The speaker, a poet, feels left behind with the old man.
evidence: It made me lonely and it made me sad To think that Amaryllis had grown old.

questions.prompt: Is this a poem about a real old woman, or about something else? Which details support each reading?
facilitatorNotes: Literally, a grieving old man has buried his wife in the woods. Symbolically, the name from poetry, the dreamlike meeting and the contrast with commerce suggest the death of an old kind of poetry. The poem lets both stand.
evidence: Once, when I wandered in the woods alone,

readings.title: The Pity of the Leaves
readings.challenge: Notice how the wind and the leaves become characters that torment a lonely old man.
readings.focus: A cold wind and dead leaves will not let an old man forget.
readings.context: Edwin Arlington Robinson sets this sonnet in a bleak November. Moors are open, windswept land; ancestral means coming down from one’s ancestors; reverberant means echoing; perforce means unavoidably; plagued means tormented.
readings.contentNote: An old man alone is haunted by memories of the dead.

excerpt.locator: “The Pity of the Leaves,” complete poem; opens “Vengeful across the cold November moors, Loud with ancestral shame there came the bleak…”; closes “…dead they were; but if the old man cried, They fluttered off like withered souls of men.”.

questions.prompt: What does the old man hear in the wind?
facilitatorNotes: Words of the past, from lips that will never speak again: the voices of people who have died. The wind is “loud with ancestral shame,” so old wrongs or regrets come back with it.
evidence: Words out of lips that were no more to speak
Loud with ancestral shame there came the bleak

questions.prompt: Find the sound words in the first eight lines. How do they make the wind seem alive?
facilitatorNotes: “Shrieked,” “shriek,” “reverberant,” “loud”: the wind even answers its own shriek, as if talking to itself, and “Vengeful” gives it a purpose, revenge. It behaves like a character, not weather.
evidence: Sad wind that shrieked, and answered with a shriek,
Vengeful across the cold November moors,

questions.prompt: How do the leaves plague him? Why do they stop, and what happens when he cries?
facilitatorNotes: They skip over the stones with a “freezing whisper,” stop “just to let him know / How dead they were,” then flutter away when he weeps, like withered souls. They remind him of death and seem to mock him, or perhaps they are ghosts of the people he remembers.
evidence: just to let him know How dead they were;
They fluttered off like withered souls of men.

questions.prompt: Why might the poem be called “The Pity of the Leaves”? Do the leaves pity him, or is the title ironic?
facilitatorNotes: The leaves seem cruel, so “pity” may be bitterly ironic. Or “pity” may mean a pitiful thing, as in “the pity of it,” since the leaves are dead and nearly forgotten like him. Accept readings that test the title against the poem.
evidence: And then there were the leaves that plagued him so!

readings.title: Aaron Stark
readings.challenge: Follow a chain of hard comparisons and decide what the final laugh reveals.
readings.focus: A sonnet builds a miser out of harsh images, then shows how he answers pity.
readings.context: One of Edwin Arlington Robinson’s portraits of townspeople, written as a sonnet. Withal means besides; morose means gloomy; renown is reputation; chary means sparing or cautious; a cur is a bad-tempered dog.

excerpt.locator: “Aaron Stark,” complete poem; opens “Withal a meagre man was Aaron Stark, -- Cursed and unkempt, shrewd, shrivelled, and…”; closes “…A sound of alien pity, touched with tears, -- And then (and only then) did Aaron laugh.”.

questions.prompt: Which comparisons tie Aaron Stark to money, and which to an animal?
facilitatorNotes: His eyes are “like little dollars in the dark,” so greed is part of his body; his words come out as if “a cur were chary of its bark,” a guarded, snapping dog.
evidence: And eyes like little dollars in the dark.
As if a cur were chary of its bark.

questions.prompt: Why is he “Glad” of his “hard renown”?
facilitatorNotes: He enjoys being disliked or feared; the reputation confirms him. Readers may see pride, or a man who has chosen loneliness as protection.
evidence: Glad for the murmur of his hard renown,

questions.prompt: Why does Aaron laugh only when he hears pity? What do you make of that laugh?
facilitatorNotes: Pity treats him as someone to be sorry for, and he rejects it. The laugh may be scorn, bitter pride or self-defence; the parenthesis stresses that nothing else amuses him. Some readers pity him more for it, others find him repellent.
evidence: A sound of alien pity, touched with tears, --
And then (and only then) did Aaron laugh.

readings.title: Charles Carville’s Eyes
readings.challenge: Compare two parts of one face and connect them to how the town listened.
readings.focus: A face that looks sad hides gladness, and a quiet man’s ideas are heard only after his death.
readings.context: Edwin Arlington Robinson often wrote sonnets about people his small town misread. Redeemed means made up for; insufficient means not enough; whims and theories are notions and ideas.

excerpt.locator: “Charles Carville’s Eyes,” complete poem; opens “A melancholy face Charles Carville had, But not so melancholy as it seemed, -- When once…”; closes “…he was dead, so those blank eyes of his Might speak them. Then we heard them, every word.”.

questions.prompt: How do Charles Carville’s eyes and mouth disagree?
facilitatorNotes: His eyes are “forever sad” and lifeless; his mouth “redeemed” them and “beamed.” People who knew him read the mouth; strangers saw only melancholy.
evidence: His eyes were sorry, but his mouth was glad.
But not so melancholy as it seemed, --

questions.prompt: What does “we were out of touch” admit about the speaker and the town?
facilitatorNotes: Many did not even hear half of what he said and ignored his ideas. The speaker counts himself among them, so the poem is partly a confession.
evidence: half of what he did say was not heard
we were out of touch

questions.prompt: How can dead eyes “speak”? Explain the last two lines.
facilitatorNotes: Only after his death did people attend to what he had thought; the blank eyes, remembered, seem to hold the meaning they missed. Readers may hear regret, or a comment on honouring people too late.
evidence: Till he was dead, so those blank eyes of his
Then we heard them, every word.

readings.title: The Dead Village
readings.challenge: Read the turn of a sonnet from what a place was to what it is.
readings.focus: Music becomes the poem’s image for a living community, and its loss comes without an explanation.
readings.context: Edwin Arlington Robinson sets this sonnet in an abandoned village. Sardis was a rich city of the ancient world that later lay in ruins; unrememberable means impossible to remember.

excerpt.locator: “The Dead Village,” complete poem; opens “Here there is death. But even here, they say, -- Here where the dull sun shines this…”; closes “…in dreams. The music failed, and then God frowned, and shut the village from His sight.”.

questions.prompt: What did the village have before “the change came,” and how does the speaker know?
facilitatorNotes: Gaiety, men, children at play, music. But “they say”: the happy past is reported, not witnessed, so even the memory is secondhand.
evidence: But even here, they say,
And there were little children here to play,

questions.prompt: How does music describe both the village’s life and its death?
facilitatorNotes: The children’s hands kept “in tune / The strings that stretch from heaven”; then the music “passed away” and “failed.” Music suggests harmony and a link with heaven, so its failure is the village’s death.
evidence: The strings that stretch from heaven
The music failed, and then

questions.prompt: The poem never says what killed the village. What does the last line add, and how should we read it?
facilitatorNotes: No plague, war or poverty is named. “God frowned” may be the speaker’s way of naming a disaster he cannot explain, a bitter accusation, or a statement of faith; readers should say which words support their reading.
evidence: God frowned, and shut the village from His sight.

readings.title: Fleming Helphenstine
readings.challenge: Follow a friendly meeting that turns in a single moment, and notice what stays unexplained.
readings.focus: Easy talk breaks into shared embarrassment that neither man can name.
readings.context: A sonnet by Edwin Arlington Robinson about a brief meeting with a stranger. Superfine means too refined; persuasion here means air or manner; chaffed means teased; clogged means stuck in the throat.

excerpt.locator: “Fleming Helphenstine,” complete poem; opens “At first I thought there was a superfine Persuasion in his face; but the free glow That…”; closes “…sounded half confused and half amazed, He dodged, -- and I have never seen him since.”.

questions.prompt: What first impression does the speaker form, and how does it change in the first eight lines?
facilitatorNotes: He suspects something too polished, then the joyful “Hollo!” wins him over, and they talk and joke like old friends.
evidence: At first I thought there was a superfine
And laughed and chaffed like any friend of mine.

questions.prompt: What happens at the turn? Find the words that show both men’s feelings.
facilitatorNotes: A “queer, quick frown,” a hard look both ways, then “strained shame” that makes both “cringe and wince.” Something passes between them that both recognise and neither names.
evidence: But soon, with a queer, quick frown, he looked at me,
With a strained shame that made us cringe and wince:

questions.prompt: Why might the speaker add “be that as it may” to the stranger’s name? What explanations does the poem leave open?
facilitatorNotes: He doubts the name, hinting the man is not what he seems. They may have recognised each other, seen something false in each other, or felt their sudden friendliness was unearned. Good answers stay with the shame and the dodge rather than inventing a plot.
evidence: He said his name was Fleming Helphenstine,
He dodged, -- and I have never seen him since.

readings.title: Reuben Bright
readings.challenge: Notice how the speaker argues against an assumption and lets actions show grief.
readings.focus: A butcher’s grief appears in plain acts rather than described feelings.
readings.context: A sonnet from Edwin Arlington Robinson’s portraits of small-town people. A sexton looks after a church and its graveyard; cedar boughs keep moths out of stored cloth; a slaughter-house is where animals are killed for meat.
readings.contentNote: A wife’s death and her husband’s grief; a slaughter-house is mentioned.

excerpt.locator: “Reuben Bright,” complete poem; opens “Because he was a butcher and thereby Did earn an honest living (and did right), I would…”; closes “…and put some chopped-up cedar boughs In with them, and tore down the slaughter-house.”.

questions.prompt: What does the speaker not want us to think about Reuben Bright, and why might a reader think it?
facilitatorNotes: That a butcher is “any more a brute than you or I.” Killing animals for a living might seem to harden a man; the speaker heads off that idea and includes the reader in the comparison.
evidence: Was any more a brute than you or I;

questions.prompt: How does the poem show Reuben’s grief? Point to actions rather than named feelings.
facilitatorNotes: He stares, shakes, cries “like a great baby” until the women cry too; afterwards he packs away the things she made with cedar to keep them. The actions carry the feeling.
evidence: And cried like a great baby half that night,
He packed a lot of things that she had made

questions.prompt: Why does he tear down the slaughter-house? Offer more than one reason and test each against the poem.
facilitatorNotes: He may be unable to face killing after facing death, or the place may be bound up with their life together, or the act may be grief that gives up his living. The poem gives no reason, so the act speaks for itself; connect it to the opening defence of the butcher.
evidence: and tore down the slaughter-house.

readings.title: The Tavern
readings.challenge: Separate what the speaker sees, what he imagines, and what nobody knows.
readings.focus: A ruined building holds a story the town can only partly tell.
readings.context: Tilbury Town is Edwin Arlington Robinson’s name for the small town of many of his poems, and John Evereldown is the title character of another poem in the book. Rank means overgrown; aglaze means glassy; a reprobate is a person of bad character.
readings.contentNote: Mentions a murdered innkeeper and calls a man a “skirt-crazed reprobate” (one who chases women). Nothing violent is described.

excerpt.locator: “The Tavern,” complete poem; opens “Whenever I go by there nowadays And look at the rank weeds and the strange grass, The…”; closes “…brushed, and scared, and all but overran That skirt-crazed reprobate, John Evereldown.”.

questions.prompt: What does the speaker see when he passes the Tavern now?
facilitatorNotes: Rank weeds, strange grass, torn blue curtains and broken glass: present facts of neglect, with the broken glass hinting at violence.
evidence: The torn blue curtains and the broken glass,

questions.prompt: What frightens him: the place itself, or something he imagines?
facilitatorNotes: He feels “as if” he saw the ghost of the murdered host. The fear comes from the past he pictures; words like “seem” and “as if” mark it as imagination.
evidence: For all the world as if I saw the ghost
Of old Ham Amory, the murdered host,

questions.prompt: What does the town actually know about the Tavern’s story, and what does the poem invite us to guess?
facilitatorNotes: Only that years ago a stranger galloped up after midnight and nearly ran down John Evereldown. Readers may connect the rider with the murder, but the poem offers no proof; good answers keep fact and guess apart.
evidence: The Tavern has a story, but no man
A stranger galloped up from Tilbury Town,

readings.title: Walt Whitman
readings.challenge: Follow a tribute that argues with itself, from “ended” to “never ended.”
readings.focus: A great poet is dead; are his songs over?
readings.context: Walt Whitman (1819–1892), the American poet of Leaves of Grass, wrote long, free-flowing lines celebrating ordinary people, democracy and the whole of life; many readers of his time disliked or ignored him. Edwin Arlington Robinson wrote this tribute in the 1890s, a few years after Whitman died, in unrhymed lines. Cadence is the rise and fall of a voice or a line of verse.

excerpt.locator: “Walt Whitman,” complete poem; opens “The master-songs are ended, and the man That sang them is a name. And so is God A name;…”; closes “…When we write Men's letters on proud marble or on sand, We write them there forever.”.

questions.prompt: The poem begins by saying that Whitman, God, love, life and death are each “a name.” What does that mean, and why is it a gloomy start?
facilitatorNotes: Once the singer is dead, he is only a name, a word without the living person; and the speaker fears that God, love and death are names too, which we are too blind to understand. All we can do is “blink, and wonder.”
evidence: The master-songs are ended, and the man That sang them is a name.
We only blink, and wonder.

questions.prompt: Explain the reversal: “Last night it was the song that was the man, / But now it is the man that is the song.”
facilitatorNotes: While Whitman lived, his songs expressed the man; now that he is dead, the man lives only in his songs. Swapping the words in the second line acts out the change it describes.
evidence: Last night it was the song that was the man, But now it is the man that is the song.

questions.prompt: Why, according to the speaker, do people “not hear him very much to-day”? Who does hear him?
facilitatorNotes: His voice is “too pure,” “too large” and too triumphant for the present. A few hear him, and they know he will sing to all people in time. Robinson, then unknown himself, may be counting himself among those few.
evidence: We do not hear him very much to-day:
That he shall sing to-morrow for all men,

questions.prompt: The last stanza begins with a question about the opening line. How does the speaker answer himself?
facilitatorNotes: He takes back “ended”: no song that has been sung ever ends, and no name is a dead name; what we write, “on proud marble or on sand,” stays forever. Sand is a surprising choice, since sand washes away; readers can debate whether that makes the claim braver or less believable.
evidence: No songs are ended that are ever sung,
Men's letters on proud marble or on sand, We write them there forever.

readings.title: The Wilderness
readings.challenge: Follow the pull between the wild and home in a poem built like a song.
readings.focus: Wanderers hear the call to go home before winter traps them.
readings.context: Edwin Arlington Robinson writes in long, swinging lines, like a sea-shanty or a marching song, with an indented refrain between the stanzas. The speakers are wanderers in wild country at the end of autumn. Shoal is shallow water; a dirge is a funeral song; languor is drowsy laziness; the roving-fiend is the restless urge to wander, pictured as a devil; enmity is hostility; to blight is to wither; rushes are tall grasses that grow by water.
readings.contentNote: The last refrain imagines frozen dead men laughing in the rushes.

excerpt.locator: “The Wilderness,” complete poem; opens “Come away! come away! there's a frost along the marshes, And a frozen wind that skims the…”; closes “…sinks and whimpers in the shrill November rushes, And the long fall wind on the lake._”.

questions.prompt: What signs of the season does the first stanza give, and how do they push the wanderers to leave?
facilitatorNotes: Frost on the marshes, a frozen wind over dead black water, a moan and a wailing “dirge” in the woods, and ashes where autumn’s crimson was. Summer’s glory has gone; the land itself seems to send them home.
evidence: Come away! come away! there's a frost along the marshes,
There is nothing left but ashes now where the crimson chills of autumn

questions.prompt: What waits for them at home, according to the refrains and the third stanza?
facilitatorNotes: The lights of home, a fire that is “young forever,” a gleaming window, a warm hearth, love, and “a faithful woman’s eyes.” Home is warmth and faithfulness, set against frost and wandering.
evidence: Are barren for the lights of home and a flame that's young forever;
In the strangeness of home-coming, and a faithful woman's eyes.

questions.prompt: Who is the “roving-fiend,” and why must they leave before he holds them?
facilitatorNotes: The restless urge to keep wandering, pictured as a devil. Once his hands close on a man, no one can leave him, and no one will admit he is an enemy. So they must go now, quietly: “the less we brag the better.”
evidence: or the roving-fiend will hold us,
There are no men yet can leave him when his hands are clutched upon them,

questions.prompt: The last refrain speaks of “dead men all around us.” How does it change the mood of the ending?
facilitatorNotes: The earlier refrains promised home; this one shows what happens to those who stayed, frozen men who mock with a hard laugh. The call becomes urgent and frightening. The dead men may also be the wind in the rushes heard as voices; the poem ends with wind, not home.
evidence: Frozen men that mock us with a wild, hard laugh
That shrieks and sinks and whimpers in the shrill November rushes,

readings.title: Romance
readings.challenge: Notice what two very short poems leave unsaid, and why the gaps matter.
readings.focus: Two glimpses of friends from long ago, each ending in silence.
readings.context: Edwin Arlington Robinson groups two very short poems under the title “Romance,” an old word for a tale of adventure or love. Each looks back at friends from the past.

excerpt.locator: “Romance,” complete (I, “Boys,” and II, “James Wetherell”); opens “We were all boys, and three of us were friends; And we were more than friends, it seemed…”; closes “…vanished from our view, -- There is n't very much to write, There is n't very much to do.”.

questions.prompt: In “Boys,” how does the speaker’s description of the three friends change from the first line to the last?
facilitatorNotes: Friends, then more than friends, then more than brothers; then a doubtful “Brothers?” and “there it ends.” The closeness belonged to boyhood and did not last.
evidence: Yes, we were more than brothers then, we three.
But we were boys, and there it ends.

questions.prompt: Which words and marks show the speaker’s doubt? What might he be feeling?
facilitatorNotes: “It seemed to me,” the trailing dots, the question “Brothers?” They suggest hesitation and perhaps hurt: something later broke the friendship, or he now sees how young they were. The poem never says which.
evidence: And we were more than friends, it seemed to me:

questions.prompt: What do we learn about James Wetherell, and what does the poem refuse to tell?
facilitatorNotes: People told stories about him that “we” never half believed; they liked him and treated him well. Now “some things have come to light” and he has vanished. We never learn what he did, or where he went.
evidence: We never half believed the stuff They told about James Wetherell;
But now some things have come to light, And James has vanished from our view,

questions.prompt: Why might Robinson call these two poems “Romance”? Is the title serious or ironic?
facilitatorNotes: Romance promises adventure and glamour, but both poems end flatly: “there it ends,” “There is n’t very much to write.” The title may be ironic, or it may mean the stories we invent about people we never really knew. Accept either if it is argued from the lines.
evidence: There is n't very much to write, There is n't very much to do.
